questions.correctAnswer: How to allocate limited resources among competing uses
distractors: How to print enough money so everyone can buy everything
How to eliminate all economic tradeoffs permanently
How to guarantee exactly equal incomes for all citizens
questions.explanation: Scarcity means unlimited wants exceed limited resources, so every society must choose how to allocate what it has.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Scarcity is why you cannot have everything - choices are mandatory!
questions.question: What does scarcity force every society to decide?

questions.correctAnswer: The value of the next-best alternative given up when a choice is made
distractors: The total money spent on every available option
The accounting cost recorded in a firm's books
The time it takes to make an economic decision
questions.explanation: Opportunity cost is what you sacrifice - the best alternative you did not choose - whenever resources are used one way instead of another.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Every yes is a no to something else - that no is your opportunity cost!
questions.question: Opportunity cost is best defined as:

questions.correctAnswer: Increasing opportunity costs as production shifts between goods
distractors: Decreasing opportunity costs as production shifts between goods
Constant unemployment of labor and capital
Government price controls on both goods
questions.explanation: Resources are not equally suited to all uses, so producing more of one good costs increasingly more of the other - the PPC is concave.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: A bowed-out PPC means each extra unit costs more than the last!
questions.question: A production possibilities curve bows outward because of:

questions.correctAnswer: Inefficient production with unemployed resources
distractors: The maximum attainable output of the economy
An impossible combination given current resources
Long-run economic growth
questions.explanation: Points inside the PPC are attainable but wasteful - the economy could produce more of at least one good without giving up the other.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Inside the curve means the economy is napping - resources sit idle!
questions.question: A point inside the production possibilities curve represents:

questions.correctAnswer: A major advance in production technology
distractors: A temporary increase in consumer spending
A movement from unemployment to full employment
A rise in the general price level
questions.explanation: New technology increases the maximum output possible from given resources, shifting the entire PPC outward - this is economic growth.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Better tech pushes the whole frontier out - growth, not just movement!
questions.question: Which event would shift a nation's production possibilities curve outward?

questions.correctAnswer: Quantity demanded falls as price rises
distractors: Quantity demanded rises as price rises
Demand always shifts right when income rises
Price has no effect on consumer behavior
questions.explanation: The law of demand describes the inverse relationship between price and quantity demanded, shown as a downward-sloping demand curve.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Price up, buying down - the demand curve always slopes down!
questions.question: The law of demand states that, other things equal:

questions.correctAnswer: Quantity supplied rises as price rises
distractors: Quantity supplied falls as price rises
Supply always shifts left when costs fall
Producers ignore price when deciding output
questions.explanation: Higher prices make production more profitable, so firms offer more - the supply curve slopes upward.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Price up, sellers show up - supply slopes up!
questions.question: The law of supply states that, other things equal:

questions.correctAnswer: A rise in consumer income, if pizza is a normal good
distractors: A fall in the price of pizza
A fall in the price of pizza ovens
A new tax on pizza restaurants
questions.explanation: Higher income shifts demand right for a normal good. A price change moves along the curve; input costs and taxes shift supply.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Only non-price factors shift the curve - price just slides along it!
questions.question: Which change would increase the DEMAND for pizza?

questions.correctAnswer: An increase in the price of steel
distractors: An increase in the price of cars
A new technology that speeds up assembly
A government subsidy paid to carmakers
questions.explanation: Higher input costs make production less profitable at every price, shifting supply left. Price changes move along the curve.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Costly steel means fewer cars - input costs shift supply!
questions.question: Which change would decrease the SUPPLY of cars?

questions.correctAnswer: A surplus, and price will be pushed downward
distractors: A shortage, and price will be pushed upward
A surplus, and price will be pushed upward
Neither a surplus nor a shortage
questions.explanation: Above equilibrium, quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded. Sellers cut prices to clear excess inventory.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Price too high? Shelves overflow and prices fall!
questions.question: If the price is above equilibrium, the market experiences:

questions.correctAnswer: A shortage, and price will be pushed upward
distractors: A surplus, and price will be pushed downward
A shortage, and price will be pushed downward
Neither a surplus nor a shortage
questions.explanation: Below equilibrium, quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied. Competition among buyers bids the price up.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Price too low? Shelves empty and buyers bid prices up!
questions.question: If the price is below equilibrium, the market experiences:

questions.correctAnswer: A persistent shortage
distractors: A persistent surplus
The market to clear normally
An increase in quantity supplied
questions.explanation: A ceiling below equilibrium holds price down, so quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied - a shortage results.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Cap the price low and goods vanish - ceilings cause shortages!
questions.question: A binding price ceiling set below equilibrium causes:

questions.correctAnswer: A persistent surplus
distractors: A persistent shortage
The market to clear normally
A decrease in quantity supplied
questions.explanation: A floor above equilibrium holds price up, so quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded - a surplus results.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Floor the price high and goods pile up - floors cause surpluses!
questions.question: A binding price floor set above equilibrium causes:

questions.correctAnswer: Percentage change in quantity demanded divided by percentage change in price
distractors: Change in price divided by change in quantity demanded
Total revenue divided by quantity sold
Percentage change in income divided by percentage change in quantity
questions.explanation: Elasticity measures responsiveness: %ΔQd / %ΔP. Values above 1 (in absolute value) mean elastic demand.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Elasticity is a ratio of percents - how much buyers flinch when price moves!
questions.question: The price elasticity of demand is calculated as:

questions.correctAnswer: Insulin for a diabetic patient
distractors: A luxury sports car
A brand-name breakfast cereal
A vacation cruise
questions.explanation: Necessities with no close substitutes have inelastic demand - buyers purchase them even when price rises.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: No substitute and must-have means buyers barely react - inelastic!
questions.question: Which good most likely has inelastic demand?

questions.correctAnswer: Fall, because quantity drops proportionally more than price rises
distractors: Rise, because the higher price dominates
Stay exactly the same
Rise, because buyers purchase more at higher prices
questions.explanation: With elastic demand, the quantity effect outweighs the price effect, so P x Q falls when price rises.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Elastic demand? Raise price and your revenue shrinks!
questions.question: If demand is elastic, a price increase will cause total revenue to:

questions.correctAnswer: An inferior good
distractors: A normal good
A substitute good
A complementary good
questions.explanation: Inferior goods (like instant noodles) see demand fall as income rises because buyers switch to better alternatives.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Richer buyers ditch it? That good is inferior!
questions.question: If consumer income rises and demand for a good falls, the good is:

questions.correctAnswer: Shift the supply of bread to the right
distractors: Shift the demand for bread to the right
Shift the supply of bread to the left
Move along the bread supply curve
questions.explanation: Lower input costs raise profitability, so bakeries supply more bread at every price - a rightward supply shift.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Cheaper workers, more bread - costs shift supply!
questions.question: A decrease in the wage paid to bakery workers would most likely:

questions.correctAnswer: Substitutes
distractors: Complements
Inferior goods
Unrelated goods
questions.explanation: Positive cross elasticity means a higher coffee price raises tea demand - buyers switch between the two.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Cross elasticity positive? They replace each other - substitutes!
questions.question: A positive cross-price elasticity of demand between tea and coffee means they are:

questions.correctAnswer: Change in quantity demanded, shown as movement along the demand curve
distractors: Decrease in demand, shown as a leftward shift of the curve
Increase in supply of gasoline
Decrease in the supply of gasoline
questions.explanation: Price changes cause movement along a fixed demand curve; only non-price factors shift the whole curve.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Price changed? Slide along the curve - do not shift it!
questions.question: A rise in the price of gasoline causing fewer gallons purchased is a:

questions.correctAnswer: Many sellers offering identical products
distractors: One seller controlling the entire market
A few sellers offering different products
Sellers who can freely set any price
questions.explanation: Perfect competition requires many buyers and sellers, identical products, and free entry - so each firm is a price taker.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Identical goods and tons of sellers? Nobody has pricing power!
questions.question: Perfect competition is best characterized by:

questions.correctAnswer: One seller with high barriers to entry
distractors: Many sellers with free entry
A few sellers watching each other closely
Sellers offering nearly identical products
questions.explanation: A monopoly has a single producer protected by barriers like patents, control of resources, or legal franchises.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: One seller plus a locked door for rivals equals monopoly!
questions.question: A monopoly is best characterized by:

questions.correctAnswer: Many sellers offering differentiated products
distractors: One seller offering a unique product
A few sellers offering identical products
Sellers who never advertise
questions.explanation: Restaurants and clothing stores compete by differentiating - each has slight market power but entry is easy.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Lots of sellers, each slightly different - monopolistic competition!
questions.question: Monopolistic competition is best characterized by:

questions.correctAnswer: A few large firms that are mutually interdependent
distractors: Countless small firms with no market power
One dominant firm facing no competition
Firms that never react to rivals' prices
questions.explanation: In an oligopoly, each firm's pricing and output decisions directly affect its few rivals, so they watch each other closely.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Few giants eyeing each other? That is oligopoly chess!
questions.question: An oligopoly is best characterized by:

questions.correctAnswer: Marginal revenue equals marginal cost
distractors: Price equals average total cost
Total revenue equals total cost
Average revenue equals average variable cost
questions.explanation: A firm maximizes profit by producing each unit whose added revenue covers its added cost - up to the point MR = MC.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Keep producing while the next unit pays for itself - MR equals MC!
questions.question: A firm maximizes profit by producing where:

questions.correctAnswer: Price falls below average variable cost
distractors: Price falls below average total cost
Marginal cost exceeds marginal revenue
Economic profit equals zero
questions.explanation: In the short run, a firm should shut down only when revenue cannot cover even its variable costs; losses smaller than fixed costs justify staying open.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Cannot even cover variable costs? Close the doors - for now!
questions.question: A firm should shut down in the short run when:

questions.correctAnswer: Zero, because entry drives price down to minimum average total cost
distractors: Positive, because barriers block new competitors
Negative, because competition is too intense
Zero, because the government caps profits
questions.explanation: Free entry lets new firms chase profits, pushing price down until it equals minimum ATC - leaving zero economic profit in the long run.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Free entry eats all the profit - long run means zero economic profit!
questions.question: In long-run perfectly competitive equilibrium, economic profit is:

questions.correctAnswer: One firm can supply the market at lower cost than two or more firms
distractors: One firm legally owns every input
The government grants a patent to one firm
Demand for the product is perfectly elastic
questions.explanation: Huge fixed costs and falling average costs (economies of scale) make a single producer most efficient - like a local water utility.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: One giant pipe is cheaper than two - nature favors one monopoly!
questions.question: A natural monopoly exists when:

questions.correctAnswer: A benefit to third parties not involved in the transaction
distractors: A cost imposed on the buyer of a product
A tax collected by the government
A benefit captured only by the seller
questions.explanation: Education creates spillover benefits for society (lower crime, better citizenship) beyond the student - a positive externality.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Your schooling helps everyone - spillover benefits are positive externalities!
questions.question: A positive externality is best described as:

questions.correctAnswer: The market produces too much of the good
distractors: The market produces too little of the good
The market produces the socially optimal amount
The government must ban the good entirely
questions.explanation: Polluters ignore costs imposed on others, so their private cost is below social cost - leading to overproduction relative to the optimum.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Polluters skip the bill and make too much - negative externality!
questions.question: With an uncorrected negative externality in production:

questions.correctAnswer: Nonrival and nonexcludable
distractors: Rival and excludable
Nonrival but excludable
Rival but nonexcludable
questions.explanation: National defense protects everyone at once (nonrival) and no one can be excluded (nonexcludable) - causing the free-rider problem.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Everyone enjoys it and nobody can be blocked - public good!
questions.question: Public goods are characterized as:

questions.correctAnswer: Price exceeds marginal cost, creating deadweight loss
distractors: Price equals marginal cost, maximizing total surplus
Output exceeds the competitive level
Consumer surplus increases
questions.explanation: A monopolist restricts output and charges P > MC, so some mutually beneficial trades never happen - the lost surplus is deadweight loss.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Monopoly prices kill good deals - that vanished surplus is deadweight loss!
questions.question: Compared to perfect competition, a monopoly results in:

questions.correctAnswer: Charging different prices to different buyers for the same good
distractors: Charging one price to every buyer
Setting price equal to marginal cost
Giving the product away for free
questions.explanation: Airlines charge business travelers more than vacationers for the same seat - capturing more consumer surplus.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Same seat, different price tag - that is price discrimination!
questions.question: Price discrimination means:

questions.correctAnswer: It depends on the demand for the final product the worker helps make
distractors: It is fixed by government wage laws
It is unrelated to product market conditions
It depends only on the worker's preferences
questions.explanation: Labor demand is derived from product demand - a popular product raises the value of workers who make it.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Nobody wants workers for nothing - labor demand derives from product demand!
questions.question: The demand for labor is called a derived demand because:

questions.correctAnswer: Marginal revenue product equals marginal factor cost
distractors: Wage equals average total cost
Marginal product equals zero
Total revenue equals total cost
questions.explanation: Hire each worker whose added revenue (MRP) covers their added cost (MFC) - the factor-market version of MR = MC.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Hire while the worker earns more than they cost - MRP equals MFC!
questions.question: A firm maximizes profit by hiring labor up to the point where:

questions.correctAnswer: It acts as a price floor in the labor market
distractors: It acts as a price ceiling in the labor market
It shifts labor demand to the right
It has no effect on employment
questions.explanation: A minimum wage above equilibrium sets a legal floor, which can create a surplus of labor (unemployment) among low-skilled workers.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Wage floor too high? Job seekers line up with no chairs!
questions.question: Economists analyze a binding minimum wage as:

questions.correctAnswer: Land, labor, capital, and entrepreneurship
distractors: Money, stocks, bonds, and credit
Supply, demand, price, and quantity
Taxes, subsidies, tariffs, and quotas
questions.explanation: These four inputs combine to produce all goods and services in an economy.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Land, labor, capital, entrepreneurship - the four ingredients of everything!
questions.question: The four factors of production are:

questions.correctAnswer: Average total cost falls as output rises over some range
distractors: Total cost stays constant as output rises
Marginal cost always exceeds average cost
Fixed costs increase with output
questions.explanation: Spreading fixed costs and specialization let big firms produce each unit cheaper - until diseconomies eventually set in.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Bigger factory, cheaper per unit - that is economies of scale!
questions.question: Economies of scale occur when:

questions.correctAnswer: Both suspects confess, though both would do better by staying silent
distractors: Both suspects stay silent and go free
One suspect confesses while the other stays silent
The police lack evidence to charge anyone
questions.explanation: Each prisoner fears the other will confess, so both confess - the Nash equilibrium is worse for both than cooperating.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Fear makes both confess - the dilemma's trap!
questions.question: In the classic prisoner's dilemma, the Nash equilibrium is:

questions.correctAnswer: Each member has an incentive to cheat by producing more
distractors: Members never want to increase production
Demand for the product is perfectly inelastic
The government enforces the agreement
questions.explanation: Like OPEC, each cartel member gains by secretly exceeding its quota - which is why cartels tend to break down.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Cheating pays each member, so cartels crumble!
questions.question: Cartels are inherently unstable because:

questions.correctAnswer: The market value of all final goods and services produced within a country in a year
distractors: The total income earned by a country's citizens abroad
The market value of all stocks traded each year
The government's total tax revenue in a year
questions.explanation: GDP counts final output produced inside the borders during the period - the broadest measure of economic activity.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Final goods, inside borders, one year - that is GDP!
questions.question: Gross Domestic Product (GDP) measures:

questions.correctAnswer: Real GDP adjusts for price changes while nominal GDP does not
distractors: Nominal GDP adjusts for price changes while real GDP does not
Real GDP always exceeds nominal GDP
Nominal GDP excludes government spending
questions.explanation: Real GDP values output at base-year prices, isolating actual production growth from inflation.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Real GDP strips out inflation - it shows true growth!
questions.question: What is the difference between real GDP and nominal GDP?

questions.correctAnswer: The sale of a used car
distractors: A newly built house
A haircut at a barbershop
A government-built bridge
questions.explanation: GDP counts only current production - used goods, financial trades, and intermediate goods are excluded to avoid double counting.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Old cars and stock trades? Not new production - excluded from GDP!
questions.question: Which transaction is NOT included in GDP?

questions.correctAnswer: (Nominal GDP / Real GDP) x 100
distractors: (Real GDP / Nominal GDP) x 100
Nominal GDP minus Real GDP
CPI multiplied by the unemployment rate
questions.explanation: The GDP deflator is a broad price index covering everything in GDP - it rises when the price level rises.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Nominal over real times 100 - the deflator reveals the price level!
questions.question: The GDP deflator is calculated as:

questions.correctAnswer: A fixed basket of goods and services bought by a typical urban household
distractors: Every good produced in the economy
Only goods bought by the government
A basket that changes every month
questions.explanation: The Bureau of Labor Statistics prices a representative basket monthly to track the cost of living via the CPI.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: CPI follows one shopping cart over time - that is the cost of living!
questions.question: The Consumer Price Index (CPI) tracks the price of:

questions.correctAnswer: It reduces what each dollar can buy
distractors: It increases the real value of savings
It helps lenders and hurts borrowers
It leaves purchasing power unchanged
questions.explanation: Inflation is a rise in the general price level, so each dollar purchases fewer goods and services.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Inflation shrinks your dollar's muscles - less buying power!
questions.question: How does unexpected inflation affect purchasing power?

questions.correctAnswer: Nominal interest rate minus the inflation rate
distractors: Nominal interest rate plus the inflation rate
Inflation rate minus the nominal rate
The nominal rate divided by the price level
questions.explanation: The real rate measures the true cost of borrowing and return on saving after removing inflation's erosion.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Subtract inflation from the nominal rate to find the real deal!
questions.question: The real interest rate equals:

questions.correctAnswer: Demand-pull comes from too much spending; cost-push comes from rising production costs
distractors: Demand-pull comes from falling wages; cost-push from rising demand
Both are caused only by government deficits
Cost-push raises output while demand-pull lowers it
questions.explanation: Too much money chasing too few goods pulls prices up; oil shocks or wage spikes push costs - and prices - up.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Pulled by spending or pushed by costs - two roads to inflation!
questions.question: What is the difference between demand-pull and cost-push inflation?

questions.correctAnswer: (Number unemployed / Labor force) x 100
distractors: (Number unemployed / Total population) x 100
(Labor force / Number employed) x 100
Number employed minus number unemployed
questions.explanation: Only people in the labor force (employed + actively seeking) count in the denominator.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Unemployed divided by labor force - the official jobless rate!
questions.question: The unemployment rate is calculated as:

questions.correctAnswer: Employed plus unemployed people
distractors: Everyone over age 16
Employed people plus discouraged workers
Everyone with a full-time job
questions.explanation: The labor force includes those working and those jobless but actively searching - discouraged workers are excluded.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Working or hunting for work? You are in the labor force!
questions.question: The labor force consists of:

questions.correctAnswer: Short-term joblessness between positions
distractors: Joblessness from obsolete skills
Joblessness caused by recessions
Permanent withdrawal from the labor force
questions.explanation: A graduate searching for a first job or a worker moving cities is frictionally unemployed - usually brief and voluntary.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Between jobs and looking around? That is frictional!
questions.question: Frictional unemployment refers to:

questions.correctAnswer: Workers' skills no longer match available jobs
distractors: A seasonal drop in tourism employment
A recession reducing overall demand
Workers quitting to find better pay
questions.explanation: Automation or industry decline strands workers whose skills are obsolete - structural unemployment lasts longer.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Skills outdated, jobs moved on - structural unemployment!
questions.question: Structural unemployment occurs when:

questions.correctAnswer: Joblessness caused by downturns in the business cycle
distractors: Joblessness from voluntary job switching
Joblessness from new technology
Joblessness among new labor market entrants
questions.explanation: When aggregate demand falls in a recession, firms lay off workers - cyclical unemployment rises and falls with GDP.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Recession hits, layoffs follow - cyclical unemployment!
questions.question: Cyclical unemployment is:

questions.correctAnswer: Frictional plus structural unemployment
distractors: Cyclical plus frictional unemployment
All unemployment including cyclical
Only long-term unemployment
questions.explanation: The natural rate is the unemployment that remains even at full employment - when cyclical unemployment is zero.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Natural rate equals frictional plus structural - always some churn!
questions.question: The natural rate of unemployment equals:

questions.correctAnswer: A 1% rise in cyclical unemployment is linked to about a 2% GDP gap
distractors: Unemployment and inflation always move together
GDP growth has no effect on unemployment
A 1% GDP gap causes 2% inflation
questions.explanation: Okun's law is an empirical rule: output below potential corresponds to unemployment above the natural rate.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Jobs lost, output lost - Okun links them two-to-one!
questions.question: Okun's law describes the relationship between:

questions.correctAnswer: They are not counted as unemployed
distractors: They are counted as fully employed
They are counted as frictionally unemployed
They raise the labor force participation rate
questions.explanation: Discouraged workers stopped searching, so they leave the labor force - making the official rate understate true joblessness.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Gave up looking? You vanish from the unemployment stats!
questions.question: How do discouraged workers affect the official unemployment rate?

questions.correctAnswer: Peak, contraction, trough, expansion
distractors: Inflation, deflation, stagnation, growth
Boom, bust, recovery, depression only
Trough, peak, inflation, recession
questions.explanation: The economy cycles through high points (peaks), downturns (contractions), low points (troughs), and recoveries (expansions).
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Peak, fall, bottom, climb - the business cycle loop!
questions.question: The four phases of the business cycle are:

questions.correctAnswer: Two consecutive quarters of falling real GDP
distractors: One month of rising unemployment
A year of high inflation
Two quarters of rising stock prices
questions.explanation: The common rule of thumb: real GDP declining for six months signals a recession.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: GDP down two quarters in a row? Recession!
questions.question: A recession is commonly defined as:

questions.correctAnswer: Real GDP divided by population
distractors: Nominal GDP divided by the price level only
Total GDP multiplied by population
GDP minus government spending
questions.explanation: Per capita output adjusts for population size, giving a rough measure of average living standards.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Split GDP among everyone - per capita living standards!
questions.question: Real GDP per capita is calculated as:

questions.correctAnswer: 70 divided by the annual growth rate
distractors: The growth rate divided by 70
70 multiplied by the growth rate
100 divided by the inflation rate
questions.explanation: At 7% growth, GDP doubles in about 10 years (70/7) - a handy approximation for compounding.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: 70 over growth rate - doubling time in a snap!
questions.question: The rule of 70 estimates doubling time as:

questions.correctAnswer: Changes in government spending and taxation to influence the economy
distractors: Changes in the money supply by the central bank
Regulation of international trade flows
Setting of interest rates by commercial banks
questions.explanation: Congress and the President use the budget - spending more or taxing less to stimulate, the reverse to cool the economy.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Congress controls the wallet - spending and taxes are fiscal policy!
questions.question: Fiscal policy refers to:

questions.correctAnswer: Increase government spending or cut taxes
distractors: Decrease government spending and raise taxes
Raise interest rates
Sell government bonds to reduce the money supply
questions.explanation: Deficit spending boosts aggregate demand, fighting recession and cyclical unemployment.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Recession? Spend more, tax less - expansionary fiscal!
questions.question: An expansionary fiscal policy would:

questions.correctAnswer: Decrease government spending or raise taxes
distractors: Increase government spending and cut taxes
Lower the required reserve ratio
Buy bonds in open market operations
questions.explanation: Surplus-leaning budgets reduce aggregate demand to fight demand-pull inflation.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Inflation raging? Spend less, tax more - contractionary fiscal!
questions.question: A contractionary fiscal policy would:

distractors: MPC / (1 - MPC)
1 / MPC
(1 - MPC) / MPC
questions.explanation: Each spending round re-spends a fraction (MPC), creating a geometric series that sums to the multiplier.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: One over one-minus-MPC - the spending multiplier!
questions.question: The government spending multiplier equals:

questions.correctAnswer: MPC + MPS = 1
distractors: MPC x MPS = 1
MPC - MPS = 1
MPC / MPS = 1
questions.explanation: Every extra dollar of income is either consumed or saved - the two propensities sum to one.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Spend it or save it - MPC plus MPS always equals one!
questions.question: The relationship between the marginal propensity to consume and to save is:

questions.correctAnswer: Part of a tax cut is saved rather than spent
distractors: Taxes are always larger than spending
The MPC is greater than one
Government spending never affects GDP
questions.explanation: A tax cut first boosts disposable income, but households save a fraction (MPS) - so the initial spending injection is smaller.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Tax cuts leak into savings first - smaller multiplier!
questions.question: The tax multiplier is smaller in absolute value than the spending multiplier because:

questions.correctAnswer: Unemployment benefits and progressive income taxes
distractors: Discretionary increases in defense spending
Annual votes to change tax rates
One-time stimulus checks only
questions.explanation: These kick in automatically - benefits rise and tax collections fall in recessions without new legislation.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: No vote needed - stabilizers fire automatically!
questions.question: Examples of automatic stabilizers include:

questions.correctAnswer: The deficit is the annual shortfall; the debt is the accumulated total owed
distractors: The debt is the annual shortfall; the deficit is the total owed
They are exactly the same thing
The deficit only includes state borrowing
questions.explanation: Each year's deficit adds to the national debt - like a bathtub's yearly inflow versus total water.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Deficit is this year's gap, debt is the whole pile!
questions.question: What is the difference between the budget deficit and the national debt?

questions.correctAnswer: Government borrowing raises interest rates, reducing private investment
distractors: Government spending directly replaces all private spending
Higher taxes always increase total investment
Deficits have no effect on interest rates
questions.explanation: Big deficits increase demand for loanable funds, pushing rates up and squeezing out business investment.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Government hogs the loan pool and rates rise - crowding out!
questions.question: The crowding-out effect occurs when:

questions.correctAnswer: Medium of exchange, store of value, and unit of account
distractors: Medium of exchange only
Store of value and barter facilitator
Unit of account and tax collector
questions.explanation: Money must be accepted in trade, hold purchasing power over time, and measure value - all three functions.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Spend it, save it, measure with it - money's three jobs!
questions.question: The three functions of money are:

questions.correctAnswer: M1 is cash plus checkable deposits; M2 adds savings and money market funds
distractors: M1 and M2 are identical measures
M1 includes savings; M2 includes only cash
M2 is narrower than M1
questions.explanation: M1 is the most liquid; M2 adds near-money assets that are slightly less liquid.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: M1 is spend-now money, M2 adds the savings cushion!
questions.question: How do the M1 and M2 money supply measures differ?

questions.correctAnswer: The Federal Reserve System
distractors: The U.S. Treasury Department
The Securities and Exchange Commission
The International Monetary Fund
questions.explanation: The Fed, created in 1913, conducts monetary policy and supervises banks.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The Fed runs the money show - central bank of the USA!
questions.question: The central bank of the United States is:

questions.correctAnswer: The fraction of deposits banks must hold and not lend
distractors: The interest rate banks charge each other
The total amount of currency in circulation
The tax rate on bank profits
questions.explanation: Banks must hold the required fraction of deposits as reserves and cannot lend that portion - the ratio caps how far lending and deposit creation can go.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Banks must keep a slice parked - that is the reserve ratio!
questions.question: The required reserve ratio is:

questions.correctAnswer: 1 / required reserve ratio
distractors: Required reserve ratio x deposits
Deposits minus required reserves
1 - required reserve ratio
questions.explanation: With a 10% ratio, each $1 of reserves can support $10 of deposits through repeated lending.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Flip the reserve ratio - that is the money multiplier!
questions.question: The simple money multiplier equals:

questions.correctAnswer: Buying and selling government bonds
distractors: Changing income tax rates
Printing currency for the Treasury
Setting the minimum wage
questions.explanation: The Fed's main tool: buying bonds injects reserves and expands the money supply; selling does the reverse.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Fed buys bonds, money floods in - open market operations!
questions.question: The Federal Reserve's primary policy tool is:

questions.correctAnswer: The rate the Fed charges banks for loans
distractors: The rate banks charge their best customers
The interest rate on government bonds
The inflation rate target
questions.explanation: Lowering the discount rate encourages bank borrowing and lending, expanding the money supply.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The Fed's own loan rate to banks - the discount rate!
questions.question: The discount rate is:

questions.correctAnswer: Lower interest rates to increase investment and aggregate demand
distractors: Raise interest rates to reduce inflation
Increase taxes to balance the budget
Sell bonds to shrink the money supply
questions.explanation: Buying bonds, cutting the discount rate, or lowering reserve requirements all push rates down and stimulate spending.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Cheap money time - expansionary monetary policy!
questions.question: An expansionary monetary policy aims to:

questions.correctAnswer: Raise interest rates to decrease aggregate demand
distractors: Lower interest rates to fight unemployment
Increase the money supply rapidly
Cut taxes to stimulate spending
questions.explanation: Selling bonds and raising rates makes borrowing costly, cooling an overheated economy.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Expensive money cools things down - contractionary monetary!
questions.question: A contractionary monetary policy aims to:

questions.correctAnswer: Vertical, because the Fed sets the quantity of money
distractors: Horizontal, because interest rates are fixed
Downward sloping, like a demand curve
Upward sloping, like a supply curve
questions.explanation: The Fed controls the money stock independently of the interest rate, so MS is drawn vertically in the money market model.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Fed fixes the quantity - money supply stands straight up!
questions.question: In the money market model, the money supply curve is:

questions.correctAnswer: Savers supply funds and borrowers demand them; the real interest rate clears the market
distractors: The Fed directly sets all interest rates
Only the government can borrow funds
Interest rates never change
questions.explanation: In this model, saving and investment decisions respond to the real interest rate, balancing saving with investment.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Savers meet borrowers at the real interest rate - loanable funds!
questions.question: In the loanable funds market:

questions.correctAnswer: The ability to produce a good at a lower opportunity cost than another producer
distractors: The ability to produce more of a good than another producer
The ability to produce a good using fewer resources
The ability to avoid all trade with other nations
questions.explanation: Even if one country is better at everything, both gain by specializing where their relative disadvantage is smallest.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Lowest opportunity cost wins the trade game - comparative advantage!
questions.question: Comparative advantage means:

questions.correctAnswer: Absolute advantage is about productivity; comparative advantage is about opportunity cost
distractors: They mean exactly the same thing
Absolute advantage is about opportunity cost instead
Comparative advantage ignores opportunity cost
questions.explanation: A country can have an absolute advantage in everything yet still benefit from trade based on comparative advantage.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Absolute is who is best, comparative is who gives up least!
questions.question: What is the difference between absolute and comparative advantage?

questions.correctAnswer: Raise domestic prices and reduce the quantity of imports
distractors: Lower domestic prices and increase imports
Have no effect on trade volumes
Eliminate all domestic production
questions.explanation: A tariff is a tax on imports that protects domestic producers but costs consumers through higher prices.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Tax the imports and shoppers pay more - tariffs!
questions.question: Tariffs on imported goods tend to:

questions.correctAnswer: A legal limit on the quantity of a good that can be imported
distractors: A tax on exported goods
A subsidy for domestic producers
An unlimited import allowance
questions.explanation: Quotas restrict supply like tariffs do, raising prices - but the extra profit goes to foreign producers or license holders.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Cap the imports and prices climb - quotas!
questions.question: An import quota is:

questions.correctAnswer: Imports exceed exports in value
distractors: Exports exceed imports in value
The currency is appreciating
The government runs a budget surplus
questions.explanation: Net exports (exports minus imports) are negative in a deficit: the value of what the nation buys from abroad exceeds the value of what it sells abroad, so Xn pulls GDP down.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Buying more than selling abroad? Trade deficit!
questions.question: A trade deficit means:

questions.correctAnswer: Foreign goods become cheaper for domestic buyers
distractors: Domestic goods become cheaper for foreigners
Exports automatically increase
The trade deficit must widen
questions.explanation: A stronger dollar buys more foreign currency, so imports cost less in dollar terms.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Strong dollar, cheap imports - currency appreciation!
questions.question: If the U.S. dollar appreciates:

questions.correctAnswer: Exports minus imports, a component of aggregate demand
distractors: Government spending minus taxes
Total exports only
Imports minus exports, excluded from GDP
questions.explanation: GDP = C + I + G + Xn, so a rise in net exports shifts aggregate demand right.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Exports minus imports feeds straight into aggregate demand!
questions.question: Net exports are defined as:

questions.correctAnswer: An inverse relationship between inflation and unemployment in the short run
distractors: A direct relationship between inflation and GDP
No relationship between inflation and unemployment
A vertical curve at the natural rate in the short run
questions.explanation: In the short run, boosting demand lowers unemployment but raises inflation - policymakers face a tradeoff.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Short run? Less joblessness costs more inflation - the tradeoff!
questions.question: The short-run Phillips curve shows:

questions.correctAnswer: Vertical at the natural rate of unemployment
distractors: Downward sloping like the short-run curve
Horizontal at zero inflation
Upward sloping with rising GDP
questions.explanation: In the long run, expected inflation adjusts fully, so unemployment returns to its natural rate at any inflation level.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Long run? The curve stands straight at the natural rate!
questions.question: The long-run Phillips curve is:

questions.correctAnswer: Rising inflation combined with rising unemployment
distractors: Falling inflation with falling unemployment
Rising GDP with falling prices
Stable prices with full employment
questions.explanation: Adverse supply shocks (like oil spikes) shift SRAS left - pushing prices up while output and employment fall.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Stagnation plus inflation - the ugly combo called stagflation!
questions.question: Stagflation is:

questions.correctAnswer: Wealth effect, interest-rate effect, and foreign-price effect
distractors: Population growth, technology, and tastes
Wages, rents, and profits
Taxes, spending, and deficits
questions.explanation: A lower price level raises real wealth, lowers rates, and cheapens exports - all boosting quantity demanded.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Three effects push AD downhill - wealth, rates, foreign prices!
questions.question: The aggregate demand curve slopes downward because of the:

questions.correctAnswer: Input prices like wages are slow to adjust
distractors: All prices adjust instantly
The money supply is fixed forever
Aggregate demand never shifts
questions.explanation: Sticky wages mean higher output prices raise profits, so firms expand production as the price level rises.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Sticky wages make SRAS slope up - profits rise with prices!
questions.question: The short-run aggregate supply curve slopes upward because:

questions.correctAnswer: Vertical at the full-employment level of output
distractors: Horizontal at the current price level
Downward sloping like demand
Upward sloping like short-run supply
questions.explanation: In the long run, wages and prices fully adjust, so output returns to potential regardless of the price level.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Long run? Output stands tall at full employment - vertical LRAS!
questions.question: The long-run aggregate supply curve is:

questions.correctAnswer: An increase in oil prices
distractors: An increase in consumer confidence
A decrease in interest rates
An increase in government spending
questions.explanation: Higher input costs shift SRAS left - the classic adverse supply shock behind 1970s stagflation.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Oil shock? SRAS lurches left - stagflation incoming!
questions.question: Which event would shift short-run aggregate supply to the left?

questions.correctAnswer: Households, firms, government, and the foreign sector exchanging goods and money
distractors: Only banks lending to the government
Only firms selling to households
Only the foreign sector trading
questions.explanation: The circular flow traces spending, income, and production looping among all sectors of the economy.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Money round and round - the circular flow never stops!
questions.question: The circular flow model shows:

questions.correctAnswer: Classical economists stress self-correction; Keynesians stress demand shortfalls and sticky prices
distractors: They agree on every policy conclusion
Classical economists favor big deficits always
Keynesians believe markets clear instantly
questions.explanation: Classicals trust flexible prices to restore full employment; Keynesians see sticky wages and advocate active stabilization.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Classicals trust the market's bounce-back, Keynesians push demand!
questions.question: How do classical and Keynesian views of the economy differ?

questions.correctAnswer: Interest rates are near zero and monetary policy loses traction
distractors: Inflation is extremely high
The government runs a surplus
Unemployment falls to zero
questions.explanation: When rates hit the floor, the Fed cannot cut further - leaving fiscal policy as the main stabilization tool.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Rates at rock bottom? Monetary policy is trapped!
questions.question: A liquidity trap occurs when:

questions.correctAnswer: Money supply times velocity equals price level times real output
distractors: Money supply plus velocity equals inflation
Velocity always equals the interest rate
Prices times output equals unemployment
questions.explanation: MV = PQ is the quantity equation - with stable velocity, money growth drives nominal GDP.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: MV equals PQ - money times speed equals prices times stuff!
questions.question: The quantity equation of money states:

questions.correctAnswer: People respond to incentives
distractors: People ignore prices completely
Government planning always works best
Scarcity does not exist
questions.explanation: A core principle: taxes, subsidies, and prices change behavior because incentives matter.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Dangle a reward and watch behavior change - incentives rule!
questions.question: Which statement best captures a core principle of economics?

questions.correctAnswer: Positive statements describe what is; normative statements prescribe what should be
distractors: Positive statements are always true; normative always false
Normative statements describe facts; positive give opinions
There is no difference between them
questions.explanation: 'Unemployment is 4%' is positive; 'unemployment should be lower' is normative - economics as science vs. policy advice.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Is versus ought - positive describes, normative prescribes!
questions.question: What is the difference between positive and normative economic statements?
